# `@mailfn/cli`

Least-privilege MailFn CLI built with `@clifn/core`.

```sh
MAILFN_URL=https://mail.example.com MAILFN_TOKEN=... mailfn inbox create --expires 3600 --idempotency-key run-123
mailfn message wait inb_123 --sender-domain example.com --subject Verify --timeout 30000
mailfn message extract inb_123 msg_123
mailfn operations --json
```

Commands cover inbox create/list/get/delete, message list/read/wait/extract, token revoke, domain create/verify, and operations. Message bodies, raw data, credentials, webhook secrets, and verification values are redacted by default. `message extract` is an explicit content action; `--show-content` explicitly opts into other content output.
# MailFn

MailFn is a reusable programmable mailbox function for products, agents, and automated tests. It accepts real email, stores the original MIME as evidence, parses normalized messages and attachments, and exposes inbox operations through a provider-neutral core, a Cloudflare runtime, a typed client, a CLI, and an MCP server.

## Packages

| Package | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `mailfn` | Small public facade for the client and core types |
| `@mailfn/core` | Domain service, contracts, memory adapters, extraction, retention, auth, threading, drafts, and operational controls |
| `@mailfn/cloudflare` | Email Worker, HTTP Worker, D1, R2, Queue, MIME, webhook, and custom-domain adapters |
| `@mailfn/client` | Typed remote client with cancellation, bounded retries, binary downloads, and typed errors |
| `@mailfn/testing` | Expiring fixtures, lifecycle hooks, OTP/link waits, and deterministic assertions |
| `@mailfn/cli` | Least-privilege command line interface built on `@clifn/core` |
| `@mailfn/mcp` | Narrow, redacted-by-default MCP tools for agents |
| `@mailfn/sendfn` | Outbound adapter that composes with SendFn instead of duplicating delivery providers |

## Quick start

```ts
import { MailFnClient } from 'mailfn';

const mail = new MailFnClient({
  baseUrl: process.env.MAILFN_URL!,
  token: process.env.MAILFN_TOKEN!,
});

const { inbox, credential } = await mail.createInbox({
  kind: 'expiring',
  expirySeconds: 60 * 60,
  idempotencyKey: `signup:${crypto.randomUUID()}`,
});

// Give inbox.address to the system under test. Use the returned scoped
// credential for subsequent inbox access; the token is shown only once.
const scoped = new MailFnClient({ baseUrl: process.env.MAILFN_URL!, token: credential.token });
const result = await scoped.waitForMessages(inbox.id, {
  senderDomain: 'example.com',
  subject: 'Verify',
  after: new Date().toISOString(),
  timeoutMs: 30_000,
});

if (result.status === 'matched') {
  const verification = await scoped.extractVerification(inbox.id, result.messages[0].id, 'otp');
  console.log(verification.value, verification.sourceMessageId);
}
```

Waiting returns a normal `{ status: "timeout", retryable: true }` result. Cancellation uses `AbortSignal`. Filters should include sender, subject, time, and expected count when tests may receive concurrent mail.

## Runtime topology

The Cloudflare adapter implements this acceptance path:

1. Email Routing calls the Email Worker.
2. The Worker validates the recipient and limits, writes raw MIME to R2, inserts a D1 message row, and enqueues a versioned parse job.
3. The Queue consumer parses MIME, writes attachment bytes to R2, normalizes content into D1, resolves the thread, and emits versioned events.
4. The HTTP Worker serves scoped inbox, message, attachment, wait, extraction, thread, draft, webhook, domain, audit, operations, usage, abuse, support, and compliance APIs.
5. The scheduled handler expires inboxes and independently enforces raw, attachment, message, and audit retention.

See [SPEC.md](./SPEC.md), [THREAT_MODEL.md](./THREAT_MODEL.md), and [OPERATIONS.md](./OPERATIONS.md) before deploying.

## Product choices

MailFn adopts the useful primitives demonstrated by [MailSlurp](https://www.mailslurp.com/docs/api/) (real inbox APIs and explicit waits), [Mailtrap Inbound Email](https://mailtrap.io/inbound-email/) (custom domains, raw/attachment evidence, webhooks, and threading), and [AgentMail](https://docs.agentmail.to/knowledge-base/inbox-capabilities) (agent-friendly inboxes, drafts, threads, and attachments). MailFn differs by keeping the domain layer portable, using an explicit Cloudflare deployment adapter, providing deterministic test helpers, and composing outbound mail through SendFn.

## Release and safety status

The package family is versioned at `0.1.0`, uses API/event version `v1`, and is registered in the repository release manifest. `npm run gate:mailfn-release` builds, tests, packs, installs, and imports every public package. The gate also runs MailFn in workerd with real local D1/R2 bindings and Email/Queue handler invocation, exercises the checked-in SendFn service, and typechecks Router-style plus framework-neutral consumers from the packed tarballs.

Public-platform mode, billing, support, and production-security approval are separate gates. They default off. Outbound is denied when public-platform mode is enabled without explicit production-security approval, and verified sender domains are required by default. This repository work does not deploy infrastructure, modify DNS, publish packages, or approve a public service.
# MailFn Threat Model

## Assets and trust boundaries

The protected assets are mailbox addresses, raw MIME, normalized bodies, attachments, verification secrets, credential and webhook secrets, sender identity evidence, audit logs, usage records, and outbound authority. Trust boundaries exist at SMTP/Email Routing ingress, HTTP authentication, D1, R2, Queue jobs, webhook consumers, DNS/Cloudflare API calls, SendFn, CLI output, and MCP tool output.

## Required controls

- Credentials are random bearer secrets, stored only as hashes, returned once, explicitly scoped, revocable, and optionally expiring. Token comparisons and admin-token checks are constant-time.
- Project/inbox ownership is checked before resource existence is disclosed. Inbox-scoped actors cannot cross inboxes or expand delegated scopes.
- Raw MIME is evidence, never executable input. Parsed HTML removes scripts, event handlers, dangerous URLs, and remote-image loads. Attachment filenames and content types are normalized; bytes are hashed.
- Size, project/inbox/sender message-rate, inbox-count, attachment-size, webhook-count, domain-count, stored-byte, and outbound limits are tenant policy, not client suggestions. Ingress counts, stored bytes, and outbound sends use durable atomic reservations.
- Every Queue job and webhook event is versioned. Inbound delivery is deduplicated before parsing. Webhooks are HMAC-signed with timestamp and delivery ID; `verifyMailFnWebhookOnce` consumes delivery IDs through a durable replay store.
- Raw, attachment, message, and audit retention clocks are independent. Deletion metadata advances only after object deletion succeeds.
- CLI and MCP surfaces redact bodies, raw data, tokens, secrets, and verification values by default. Explicit extraction is auditable.
- Custom-domain routing is enabled only after DNS verification, exact zone-ID/name authorization, and explicit Email Routing enablement. Rule creation is idempotent and persistence failure compensates by deleting the provider rule. Public outbound requires separate production-security approval and verified sender domains.
- Errors and audits never include bearer tokens, webhook secrets, raw MIME, message bodies, or extracted verification values.

## Abuse cases

- Address enumeration: use generic recipient rejection reasons and avoid cross-tenant resource disclosure.
- Inbox flooding/storage exhaustion: apply hourly ingress, size, stored-byte, and active-inbox quotas before expensive parsing. Abuse signals lower durable sender reputation, and blocked senders are rejected before storage.
- Open relay/spam: no SMTP submission exists in core; outbound requires SendFn, `send:write`, daily quota, platform approval, and domain policy.
- Verification-code theft: source attribution, least-privilege inbox tokens, short-lived test inboxes, no-store responses, and redacted agent surfaces.
- MIME parser exploits/tracking: treat parser as untrusted boundary, preserve raw separately, sanitize display HTML, block remote images, and cap attachment sizes.
- Webhook SSRF/exfiltration: dispatch resolves A/AAAA evidence, rejects non-public destinations and redirects, and still requires a production egress policy to close DNS-rebinding races; secrets are encrypted at rest and delivery failure cannot roll back mail.
- Replay/duplicate delivery: unique provider-delivery constraint, signed webhook timestamp/delivery ID, and idempotency keys.
- DNS takeover or routing mistakes: require expected-record verification, scoped Cloudflare token, explicit routing creation, and reversible disable.

## Public launch checklist

Public launch remains blocked until production-security approval is explicitly set after external review of tenant isolation, egress/SSRF policy, domain ownership, abuse response, billing enforcement, support operations, compliance/data residency, deletion evidence, alert routing, incident runbooks, and any IMAP/SMTP/JMAP compatibility service. Code defaults alone do not satisfy those reviews.
# MailFn consumer contracts

These compile-only fixtures keep the reusable boundary honest:

- `router-cloudflare.ts` models Router's Cloudflare Worker service shape and composes MailFn with SendFn without importing MailFn internals.
- `framework-neutral.ts` proves an unrelated application can use the provider-neutral in-memory core and typed HTTP client.

The MailFn release gate copies both fixtures into the clean tarball-install project and typechecks them there. They are validation inputs, not published packages and not production deployment configuration.
# `@mailfn/cloudflare`

Cloudflare runtime adapter for MailFn: Email Worker ingress, Worker HTTP API, D1 store/migrations, R2 object storage, Queue producer/consumer, `postal-mime` parsing, signed webhooks, scheduled retention, and Cloudflare Email Routing custom-domain operations.

```ts
import { createMailFnCloudflareHandlers } from '@mailfn/cloudflare';

export default createMailFnCloudflareHandlers({
  // Optional: sendAdapter: createSendFnAdapter(sendfn)
});
```

Copy `wrangler.example.jsonc`, provision the declared bindings, apply `migrations/0001_mailfn.sql`, and set a 32-byte `MAILFN_SECRET_KEY`. `MAILFN_STORAGE_REGION` must match the D1/R2 deployment location. `MAILFN_ADMIN_TOKEN` protects initial `POST /v1/admin/projects`; set `MAILFN_PROJECT_ID` after bootstrap. Custom domains require an exact `CLOUDFLARE_ZONE_ID` plus `CLOUDFLARE_ZONE_NAME`. Public-platform, production-security, billing, and support flags default off.

Raw MIME is committed to R2 before the D1 row; the Queue job is sent last. Queue failures leave a reconcilable `queue_failed` row. Email ingress permanently rejects unknown/inactive/oversize/policy recipients and throws transient storage/Queue failures for retry. See the parent `OPERATIONS.md` and `THREAT_MODEL.md` before deployment.

The package test command includes Node unit tests and a workerd integration suite using real local D1 and R2 bindings, Email/Queue handler invocation, D1 batch atomicity, durable webhook replay, and concurrent quota enforcement. A real Cloudflare Email Routing/DNS smoke remains an approval-gated pre-runtime-release operation.

name: create-pr-ghother
description: Create or update a GitHub pull request using `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other`, especially when the current worktree is dirty or based on the wrong branch. Use this when the user wants a PR against a specific remote and branch such as `origin/dev` or `next/next`, needs `.conduct` included or excluded based on target, wants branch/title prefixing, or needs a clean temporary worktree to avoid dragging unrelated history into the PR.
---

# Create PR GH Other

## Overview

Use this skill when the user wants a PR created with the `gh-other` GitHub profile and the result must be clean, accurately described, and targeted to a specific remote and branch.

This skill exists to avoid four recurring failure modes:
- pushing from the wrong branch ancestry
- creating vague or misleading PR titles and descriptions
- accidentally including `.conduct` content in the wrong target
- leaking generated/build artifacts because `.gitignore` was not checked before staging

## Required Inputs

- target remote and target branch
  - common: `origin/dev`
  - common: `next/next`
- optional prefix for both branch name and PR title
- the current worktree containing the intended changes

If the user gives only a branch name like `dev`, assume `origin/dev`.
If the user gives only `next`, assume `next/next`.

## Hard Rules

- Always set `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other` on every `gh` command.
- Do not create forks.
- Do not create extra remotes.
- Push to the provided remote only.
- If permission is denied for that remote/repository, abort and report the denial. Do not fall back to a fork or a different remote.
- If the target is `origin/dev`, do not push `.conduct` contents.
- If the target is `next/next`, include `.conduct` contents.
- Before staging, scan the changed content for files that should be gitignored and update `.gitignore` first.
- Do not generate a PR title/body from guesswork. Read the actual changed files and make the title/body reflect the real scope.

## Workflow

### 1. Inspect The Current Worktree Thoroughly

Start by understanding what actually changed.

Run and inspect at minimum:

```bash
git status --short
git branch --show-current
git remote -v
git fetch <target-remote> <target-branch>
git rev-list --left-right --count <target-remote>/<target-branch>...HEAD
git diff --stat
git diff --name-status
```

Then read the high-signal changed files, not just filenames:

- source files
- tests
- examples
- docs
- package manifests
- `.gitignore`

Do this before drafting the branch name, commit message, PR title, or PR body.

### 2. Decide Whether A Clean Temporary Worktree Is Required

Use the current worktree branch only if it is already a clean PR base for the target branch.

Create a temporary clean worktree from `<target-remote>/<target-branch>` if any of these are true:

- the current branch is far ahead/behind the target branch
- the branch contains unrelated commits
- the user’s changes are mixed into an old branch
- a direct PR from the current branch would drag in unrelated history

When a clean worktree is needed:

1. create a temporary worktree from the target branch
2. replay the user’s intended changes into it
3. use that temporary worktree branch for commit, push, and PR

### 3. Replay Changes Safely

When replaying onto a clean worktree:

- For modified tracked files:
  - prefer patch-based replay over full-file copying
  - preserve upstream target-branch fixes
  - do not overwrite a newer target file wholesale unless the file is clearly example-only or entirely owned by the current change
- For brand-new files and directories:
  - copy them directly
- After replay:
  - run `git status --short`
  - confirm the staged/unstaged set still matches the intended scope

If replay causes conflicts or unexpected test regressions, resolve them before continuing. Do not silently ship the broken replay.

### 4. Apply `.conduct` Policy Before Staging

Target-specific policy:

- `origin/dev`
  - exclude `.conduct` contents from the PR
  - if needed, stage with explicit exclusions rather than hoping they stay out
- `next/next`
  - include `.conduct` contents

Do not decide this ad hoc. The target determines the policy.

### 5. Scan For Gitignore Candidates Before Staging

Before `git add`, inspect the full changed/untracked set for generated or machine-local files.

Check:

```bash
git status --short
git ls-files --others --exclude-standard
```

Common artifacts to catch:

- `node_modules/`
- `.build/`
- `.swiftpm/`
- `DerivedData/`
- `**/xcuserdata/`
- `**/*.xcuserstate`
- build outputs like `dist/`, `build/`, generated `.js`, `.d.ts`, source maps
- temporary verification symlinks
- cache folders created during testing

If ignore rules are missing, update `.gitignore` before staging.

Do not stage generated artifacts and then “remember to remove them later”.

### 6. Stage Only The Intended Scope

After `.gitignore` is correct and the replay is settled:

- stage only the files meant for the PR
- verify `.conduct` inclusion/exclusion again
- verify that no machine-local or generated artifacts are staged

Run:

```bash
git status --short
git diff --cached --stat
```

If a temporary verification helper was added, like a root `node_modules` symlink, remove it before commit unless it is intentionally part of the change.

### 7. Verify On The PR Branch

Run the relevant tests from the branch that will actually be pushed.

Do not rely only on tests run from the original worktree if the PR branch was rebuilt in a temporary worktree.

At minimum, run the tests that match the touched packages or the user’s requested verification scope.

### 8. Create Branch Name, Commit Message, PR Title, And PR Body From The Actual Diff

Branch naming:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the branch name with it
- otherwise use a concise branch name that reflects the real change

Default branch pattern:

```text
<prefix>/<slug>
```

or, if no prefix is provided:

```text
codex/<slug>
```

Title rules:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the PR title too
- mention the real primary areas changed
- do not collapse broad runtime work into a narrow feature label

Examples of what the title/body must capture when present:

- `datafn/swift`
- `datafn/swift-bridge`
- `searchfn/swift`
- example apps
- docs and regression coverage

Body rules:

- summarize the real change areas
- mention included packages/directories when the PR is broad
- list the tests actually run
- explicitly note `.conduct` inclusion or exclusion based on target

### 9. Push Using The Provided Remote Only

Derive the repository from the provided remote:

```bash
git remote get-url <target-remote>
```

Push the branch to that remote only.

Preferred approach:

- use the provided remote/repository
- use the `gh-other` auth context for PR creation
- if push permission is denied for that remote, stop and report the denial

Do not:

- add a new remote
- create a fork
- push to a personal repository
- silently change the destination repository

### 10. Create The PR And Verify The Live Metadata

Create the PR with:

- `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other`
- the requested base remote + branch
- the pushed branch on the provided remote

After creation, immediately inspect the live PR:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr view <number-or-url> --json title,body,url,baseRefName,headRefName
```

Confirm that:

- the title matches the real scope
- the body reflects the actual work
- the correct remote/branch were used

If the live title/body are off, fix them before reporting success:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr edit ...
```

## Learnings To Carry Forward

- Check branch ancestry before doing anything else. An old branch can make a perfectly valid code change produce a terrible PR.
- Use a clean temporary worktree when the source branch is not a clean base for the target branch.
- Replay tracked file changes as patches whenever possible; full-file copying can wipe out newer target-branch fixes.
- Read enough of the changed files to describe the real work. Titles like “native-backed search” are wrong if the PR actually adds `datafn/swift` core runtime.
- Decide `.conduct` policy from the target branch up front, not at the end.
- Scan for ignore-worthy artifacts before staging. This is when `.build`, `.swiftpm`, `DerivedData`, `xcuserdata`, and verification symlinks are easiest to catch.
- Never stage temporary verification helpers such as `node_modules` symlinks.
- After PR creation, verify the live PR metadata. Do not assume the first draft title/body is good enough.

## Final Response Requirements

When the skill completes, report:

- PR URL
- pushed branch name
- target remote/branch
- whether `.conduct` was included or excluded
- whether `.gitignore` changed and why
- tests run on the pushed branch
- any abort reason if permissions or remote policy blocked completion

# AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

## 🔧 Development Workflow

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- TypeScript + Python SDKs

### DrawFn

- Cross-framework drawing canvas
- React and Svelte adapters
- Scene management, export capabilities
- Tolerant parsing with version validation

### PlugFn

- Self-hosted integration platform
- 75+ provider integrations (GitHub, Slack, Discord, Linear, Stripe)
- OAuth 2.0 flow handling
- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

### SearchFn

- Browser-first full-text search
- IndexedDB persistence with in-memory LRU cache
- BM25 scoring
- FlexSearch-compatible API
- Worker-ready with snapshot export/import

### CacheFn

- Multi-tier caching (memory, IndexedDB, external)
- Function memoization
- TTL and invalidation strategies
- Browser and server support

### SecFn

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting
- Security monitoring
- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

# Run for specific package
turbo run build --filter=authfn

# Run with dependencies
turbo run build --filter=authfn...

# Clear cache
turbo run clean
```

## 📚 Important Files

### Root Configuration

- `package.json` - Workspace and script definitions
- `turbo.json` - Turbo build configuration
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript base config (if exists)

### Package Configuration

- `package.json` - Package metadata, dependencies, scripts

- `pyproject.toml` - Python package configuration

### Documentation

## 🔍 Finding Code

### Search Patterns

- **Function implementations**: `{function}/typescript/src/` or `{function}/python/{function}/`
- **Tests**: `__tests__/`, `tests/`, `*.test.ts`, `test_*.py`
- **Types**: `types.ts`, `models.py`, `src/types/`
- **Adapters**: `packages/http-*/`, `packages/python-*/`, `adapters/`
- **Examples**: `examples/`, `{function}/examples/`

### Key Directories

```
superfunctions/
├── {function}/              # Core function packages
│   ├── typescript/          # TS implementation
│   ├── python/              # Python implementation
│   ├── .conduct/            # Artifacts
│   ├── README.md            # Documentation
│   └── SPEC.md              # Specification (if exists)
├── packages/                # Shared packages
│   ├── {name}/              # @superfunctions/{name}
│   └── python-{name}/       # Python shared packages
└── _conduct/                # Root artifacts
```

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety
- Provide Python SDKs for backend-focused functions
- Write comprehensive tests

### Documentation

- Update README.md with usage examples
- Create SPEC.md for complex functions
- Document breaking changes
- Keep artifacts in `.conduct/` folders

### Testing

- Use Vitest for TypeScript
- Use pytest for Python
- Maintain high test coverage
- Test adapters separately

### Versioning

- Follow semantic versioning
- Coordinate versions across language SDKs
- Document migration guides for breaking changes

2. **Respect the naming conventions** - shared packages use `@superfunctions/`, functions use simple names
3. **Create artifacts in `.conduct/` folders**, not in root or arbitrary locations
4. **Avoid nested monorepos** - use subfolders within the main Turbo monorepo
5. **Use Turbo commands** for cross-package operations
6. **Check existing patterns** in similar functions before implementing new features
7. **Maintain consistency** across TypeScript and Python SDKs
8. **Update workspaces** in root `package.json` when adding new packages
9. **Follow existing test patterns** (Vitest for TS, pytest for Python)
10. **Document thoroughly** - this is a developer-focused ecosystem

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

## 🔧 Development Workflow

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- TypeScript + Python SDKs

### DrawFn

- Cross-framework drawing canvas
- React and Svelte adapters
- Scene management, export capabilities
- Tolerant parsing with version validation

### PlugFn

- Self-hosted integration platform
- 75+ provider integrations (GitHub, Slack, Discord, Linear, Stripe)
- OAuth 2.0 flow handling
- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

### SearchFn

- Browser-first full-text search
- IndexedDB persistence with in-memory LRU cache
- BM25 scoring
- FlexSearch-compatible API
- Worker-ready with snapshot export/import

### CacheFn

- Multi-tier caching (memory, IndexedDB, external)
- Function memoization
- TTL and invalidation strategies
- Browser and server support

### SecFn

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting
- Security monitoring
- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

# Run for specific package
turbo run build --filter=authfn

# Run with dependencies
turbo run build --filter=authfn...

# Clear cache
turbo run clean
```

## 📚 Important Files

### Root Configuration

- `package.json` - Workspace and script definitions
- `turbo.json` - Turbo build configuration
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript base config (if exists)

### Package Configuration

- `package.json` - Package metadata, dependencies, scripts
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript configuration
- `vitest.config.ts` - Test configuration
- `pyproject.toml` - Python package configuration

### Documentation

- `README.md` - Package overview and usage
- `SPEC.md` - Technical specification (common in larger functions)
- `.conduct/*.md` - Implementation plans, audits, tasks

## 🔍 Finding Code

### Search Patterns

- **Function implementations**: `{function}/typescript/src/` or `{function}/python/{function}/`
- **Tests**: `__tests__/`, `tests/`, `*.test.ts`, `test_*.py`
- **Types**: `types.ts`, `models.py`, `src/types/`
- **Adapters**: `packages/http-*/`, `packages/python-*/`, `adapters/`
- **Examples**: `examples/`, `{function}/examples/`

### Key Directories

```
superfunctions/
├── {function}/              # Core function packages
│   ├── typescript/          # TS implementation
│   ├── python/              # Python implementation
│   ├── .conduct/            # Artifacts
│   ├── README.md            # Documentation
│   └── SPEC.md              # Specification (if exists)
├── packages/                # Shared packages
│   ├── {name}/              # @superfunctions/{name}
│   └── python-{name}/       # Python shared packages
└── _conduct/                # Root artifacts
```

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety
- Provide Python SDKs for backend-focused functions
- Write comprehensive tests

### Documentation

- Update README.md with usage examples
- Create SPEC.md for complex functions
- Document breaking changes
- Keep artifacts in `.conduct/` folders

### Testing

- Use Vitest for TypeScript
- Use pytest for Python
- Maintain high test coverage
- Test adapters separately

### Versioning

- Follow semantic versioning
- Coordinate versions across language SDKs
- Document migration guides for breaking changes

## 🔗 Related Resources

- **Repository**: https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions
- **License**: MIT (most packages) / Apache-2.0 (some packages)
- **Organization**: 21n
- **Contact**: hello@21n.org

## 📝 Notes for AI Agents

1. **Always check both TypeScript and Python** implementations when working on core functions
2. **Respect the naming conventions** - shared packages use `@superfunctions/`, functions use simple names
3. **Create artifacts in `.conduct/` folders**, not in root or arbitrary locations
4. **Avoid nested monorepos** - use subfolders within the main Turbo monorepo
5. **Use Turbo commands** for cross-package operations
6. **Check existing patterns** in similar functions before implementing new features
7. **Maintain consistency** across TypeScript and Python SDKs
8. **Update workspaces** in root `package.json` when adding new packages
9. **Follow existing test patterns** (Vitest for TS, pytest for Python)
10. **Document thoroughly** - this is a developer-focused ecosystem

---

**Last Updated**: 2026-01-12
**Monorepo Version**: 0.1.0
**Package Manager**: npm@10.2.0
**Build Tool**: Turbo v2.0.0

name: create-pr-ghother
description: Create or update a GitHub pull request using `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other`, especially when the current worktree is dirty or based on the wrong branch. Use this when the user wants a PR against a specific remote and branch such as `origin/dev` or `next/next`, needs `.conduct` included or excluded based on target, wants branch/title prefixing, or needs a clean temporary worktree to avoid dragging unrelated history into the PR.
---

# Create PR GH Other

## Overview

Use this skill when the user wants a PR created with the `gh-other` GitHub profile and the result must be clean, accurately described, and targeted to a specific remote and branch.

This skill exists to avoid four recurring failure modes:
- pushing from the wrong branch ancestry
- creating vague or misleading PR titles and descriptions
- accidentally including `.conduct` content in the wrong target
- leaking generated/build artifacts because `.gitignore` was not checked before staging

## Required Inputs

- target remote and target branch
  - common: `origin/dev`
  - common: `next/next`
- optional prefix for both branch name and PR title
- the current worktree containing the intended changes

If the user gives only a branch name like `dev`, assume `origin/dev`.
If the user gives only `next`, assume `next/next`.

## Hard Rules

- Always set `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other` on every `gh` command.
- Do not create forks.
- Do not create extra remotes.
- Push to the provided remote only.
- If permission is denied for that remote/repository, abort and report the denial. Do not fall back to a fork or a different remote.
- If the target is `origin/dev`, do not push `.conduct` contents.
- If the target is `next/next`, include `.conduct` contents.
- Before staging, scan the changed content for files that should be gitignored and update `.gitignore` first.
- Do not generate a PR title/body from guesswork. Read the actual changed files and make the title/body reflect the real scope.

## Workflow

### 1. Inspect The Current Worktree Thoroughly

Start by understanding what actually changed.

Run and inspect at minimum:

```bash
git status --short
git branch --show-current
git remote -v
git fetch <target-remote> <target-branch>
git rev-list --left-right --count <target-remote>/<target-branch>...HEAD
git diff --stat
git diff --name-status
```

Then read the high-signal changed files, not just filenames:

- source files
- tests
- examples
- docs
- package manifests
- `.gitignore`

Do this before drafting the branch name, commit message, PR title, or PR body.

### 2. Decide Whether A Clean Temporary Worktree Is Required

Use the current worktree branch only if it is already a clean PR base for the target branch.

Create a temporary clean worktree from `<target-remote>/<target-branch>` if any of these are true:

- the current branch is far ahead/behind the target branch
- the branch contains unrelated commits
- the user’s changes are mixed into an old branch
- a direct PR from the current branch would drag in unrelated history

When a clean worktree is needed:

1. create a temporary worktree from the target branch
2. replay the user’s intended changes into it
3. use that temporary worktree branch for commit, push, and PR

### 3. Replay Changes Safely

When replaying onto a clean worktree:

- For modified tracked files:
  - prefer patch-based replay over full-file copying
  - preserve upstream target-branch fixes
  - do not overwrite a newer target file wholesale unless the file is clearly example-only or entirely owned by the current change
- For brand-new files and directories:
  - copy them directly
- After replay:
  - run `git status --short`
  - confirm the staged/unstaged set still matches the intended scope

If replay causes conflicts or unexpected test regressions, resolve them before continuing. Do not silently ship the broken replay.

### 4. Apply `.conduct` Policy Before Staging

Target-specific policy:

- `origin/dev`
  - exclude `.conduct` contents from the PR
  - if needed, stage with explicit exclusions rather than hoping they stay out
- `next/next`
  - include `.conduct` contents

Do not decide this ad hoc. The target determines the policy.

### 5. Scan For Gitignore Candidates Before Staging

Before `git add`, inspect the full changed/untracked set for generated or machine-local files.

Check:

```bash
git status --short
git ls-files --others --exclude-standard
```

Common artifacts to catch:

- `node_modules/`
- `.build/`
- `.swiftpm/`
- `DerivedData/`
- `**/xcuserdata/`
- `**/*.xcuserstate`
- build outputs like `dist/`, `build/`, generated `.js`, `.d.ts`, source maps
- temporary verification symlinks
- cache folders created during testing

If ignore rules are missing, update `.gitignore` before staging.

Do not stage generated artifacts and then “remember to remove them later”.

### 6. Stage Only The Intended Scope

After `.gitignore` is correct and the replay is settled:

- stage only the files meant for the PR
- verify `.conduct` inclusion/exclusion again
- verify that no machine-local or generated artifacts are staged

Run:

```bash
git status --short
git diff --cached --stat
```

If a temporary verification helper was added, like a root `node_modules` symlink, remove it before commit unless it is intentionally part of the change.

### 7. Verify On The PR Branch

Run the relevant tests from the branch that will actually be pushed.

Do not rely only on tests run from the original worktree if the PR branch was rebuilt in a temporary worktree.

At minimum, run the tests that match the touched packages or the user’s requested verification scope.

### 8. Create Branch Name, Commit Message, PR Title, And PR Body From The Actual Diff

Branch naming:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the branch name with it
- otherwise use a concise branch name that reflects the real change

Default branch pattern:

```text
<prefix>/<slug>
```

or, if no prefix is provided:

```text
codex/<slug>
```

Title rules:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the PR title too
- mention the real primary areas changed
- do not collapse broad runtime work into a narrow feature label

Examples of what the title/body must capture when present:

- `datafn/swift`
- `datafn/swift-bridge`
- `searchfn/swift`
- example apps
- docs and regression coverage

Body rules:

- summarize the real change areas
- mention included packages/directories when the PR is broad
- list the tests actually run
- explicitly note `.conduct` inclusion or exclusion based on target

### 9. Push Using The Provided Remote Only

Derive the repository from the provided remote:

```bash
git remote get-url <target-remote>
```

Push the branch to that remote only.

Preferred approach:

- use the provided remote/repository
- use the `gh-other` auth context for PR creation

const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd:"GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr create --repo 21nCo/super-functions.next --base next --head codex/sfn-17-mailfn --title 'feat(mailfn): add reusable programmable mailbox function' --body '## Summary

- add the public MailFn package family: `@mailfn/core`, `@mailfn/cloudflare`, `@mailfn/client`, `@mailfn/testing`, `@mailfn/cli`, `@mailfn/mcp`, `@mailfn/sendfn`, and the `mailfn` facade
- implement provider-neutral inbox lifecycle, scoped credentials, waits and extraction, raw MIME and attachment evidence, threading, drafts, labels, search, webhooks, custom domains, retention, quotas, audit, operations, and gated public-platform controls
- add the Cloudflare Email Worker, D1, R2, Queue, HTTP, scheduled-retention, and workerd integration surface
- compose outbound drafts through SendFn with stable idempotency keys and safe stale-pending recovery while preserving current push and WhatsApp behavior
- register MailFn in workspaces, releases, ecosystem docs, CI, operations, threat-model, and Conduct artifacts

MailFn adopts selected programmable-mailbox primitives from MailSlurp, Mailtrap Inbound Email, and AgentMail without claiming parity with their hosted control planes, deliverability systems, or support operations.

Linear: [SFN-17](https://linear.app/21n/issue/SFN-17/build-mailfn-as-a-reusable-programmable-mailbox-function)

## Validation

- Node 22.22.0: `npm ci --no-audit --no-fund`
- Node 22.22.0: `npm run gate:mailfn-release`
  - 88 MailFn tests and 61 SendFn tests
  - package builds and Cloudflare workerd integration
  - MCP stdio process probe
  - npm pack, clean install, and import of all eight public packages
  - Router-style and framework-neutral consumer typechecks
- SQLite executes `mailfn/cloudflare/migrations/0001_mailfn.sql` and creates the complete D1 schema
- `git diff --check`

## Known baseline checks

- `docs/npm run check:catalog` still reports the existing duplicate `http-openapi` and `oauth-router` entries plus the existing `python-core` package-name mismatch; all MailFn-specific catalog result sets are clean
- root `npm ls` still reports existing monorepo peer and workspace-version noise; the clean install and scoped MailFn release gate pass

## Release boundaries

This PR does not deploy Cloudflare infrastructure, modify DNS, publish npm packages, perform real mail delivery, authorize public-platform mode, or prove the separate seven-day production observation gate.

`.conduct` artifacts are included because the target is `sf-next/next`.'",workdir:"/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/worktrees/superfunctions/mailfn",yield_time_ms:30000,max_output_tokens:20000});

content.text: The repair solved Rollup, and CI then exposed why `npm install --no-save` was too broad: it re-resolved the workspace and upgraded Vitest from the lockfile’s 3.2.4 to 3.2.7, creating an internal-package mismatch in workerd. I’m replacing that step with a targeted `npm pack` + extraction of only the Rollup native tarball, which leaves the `npm ci` dependency graph byte-for-byte intact.

- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

## 🔧 Development Workflow

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- TypeScript + Python SDKs

### DrawFn

- Cross-framework drawing canvas
- React and Svelte adapters
- Scene management, export capabilities
- Tolerant parsing with version validation

### PlugFn

- Self-hosted integration platform
- 75+ provider integrations (GitHub, Slack, Discord, Linear, Stripe)
- OAuth 2.0 flow handling
- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

### SearchFn

- Browser-first full-text search
- IndexedDB persistence with in-memory LRU cache
- BM25 scoring
- FlexSearch-compatible API
- Worker-ready with snapshot export/import

### CacheFn

- Multi-tier caching (memory, IndexedDB, external)
- Function memoization
- TTL and invalidation strategies
- Browser and server support

### SecFn

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting
- Security monitoring
- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

# Run for specific package
turbo run build --filter=authfn

# Run with dependencies
turbo run build --filter=authfn...

# Clear cache
turbo run clean
```

## 📚 Important Files

### Root Configuration

- `package.json` - Workspace and script definitions
- `turbo.json` - Turbo build configuration
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript base config (if exists)

### Package Configuration

- `package.json` - Package metadata, dependencies, scripts
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript configuration
- `vitest.config.ts` - Test configuration
- `pyproject.toml` - Python package configuration

### Documentation

- `README.md` - Package overview and usage
- `SPEC.md` - Technical specification (common in larger functions)
- `.conduct/*.md` - Implementation plans, audits, tasks

## 🔍 Finding Code

### Search Patterns

- **Function implementations**: `{function}/typescript/src/` or `{function}/python/{function}/`
- **Tests**: `__tests__/`, `tests/`, `*.test.ts`, `test_*.py`
- **Types**: `types.ts`, `models.py`, `src/types/`
- **Adapters**: `packages/http-*/`, `packages/python-*/`, `adapters/`
- **Examples**: `examples/`, `{function}/examples/`

### Key Directories

```
superfunctions/
├── {function}/              # Core function packages
│   ├── typescript/          # TS implementation
│   ├── python/              # Python implementation
│   ├── .conduct/            # Artifacts
│   ├── README.md            # Documentation
│   └── SPEC.md              # Specification (if exists)
├── packages/                # Shared packages
│   ├── {name}/              # @superfunctions/{name}
│   └── python-{name}/       # Python shared packages
└── _conduct/                # Root artifacts
```

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety
- Provide Python SDKs for backend-focused functions
- Write comprehensive tests

### Documentation

- Update README.md with usage examples
- Create SPEC.md for complex functions
- Document breaking changes
- Keep artifacts in `.conduct/` folders

### Testing

- Use Vitest for TypeScript
- Use pytest for Python
- Maintain high test coverage
- Test adapters separately

### Versioning

- Follow semantic versioning
- Coordinate versions across language SDKs
- Document migration guides for breaking changes

## 🔗 Related Resources

- **Repository**: https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions
- **License**: MIT (most packages) / Apache-2.0 (some packages)
- **Organization**: 21n
- **Contact**: hello@21n.org

## 📝 Notes for AI Agents

1. **Always check both TypeScript and Python** implementations when working on core functions
2. **Respect the naming conventions** - shared packages use `@superfunctions/`, functions use simple names
3. **Create artifacts in `.conduct/` folders**, not in root or arbitrary locations
4. **Avoid nested monorepos** - use subfolders within the main Turbo monorepo
5. **Use Turbo commands** for cross-package operations
6. **Check existing patterns** in similar functions before implementing new features
7. **Maintain consistency** across TypeScript and Python SDKs
8. **Update workspaces** in root `package.json` when adding new packages
9. **Follow existing test patterns** (Vitest for TS, pytest for Python)
10. **Document thoroughly** - this is a developer-focused ecosystem

    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

## 🔧 Development Workflow

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- TypeScript + Python SDKs

### DrawFn

- Cross-framework drawing canvas
- React and Svelte adapters
- Scene management, export capabilities
- Tolerant parsing with version validation

### PlugFn

- Self-hosted integration platform
- 75+ provider integrations (GitHub, Slack, Discord, Linear, Stripe)
- OAuth 2.0 flow handling
- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

### SearchFn

- Browser-first full-text search
- IndexedDB persistence with in-memory LRU cache
- BM25 scoring
- FlexSearch-compatible API
- Worker-ready with snapshot export/import

### CacheFn

- Multi-tier caching (memory, IndexedDB, external)
- Function memoization
- TTL and invalidation strategies
- Browser and server support

### SecFn

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting
- Security monitoring
- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

# Run for specific package
turbo run build --filter=authfn

# Run with dependencies
turbo run build --filter=authfn...

# Clear cache
turbo run clean
```

## 📚 Important Files

### Root Configuration

- `package.json` - Workspace and script definitions
- `turbo.json` - Turbo build configuration
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript base config (if exists)

### Package Configuration

- `package.json` - Package metadata, dependencies, scripts
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript configuration
- `vitest.config.ts` - Test configuration
- `pyproject.toml` - Python package configuration

### Documentation

- `README.md` - Package overview and usage
- `SPEC.md` - Technical specification (common in larger functions)
- `.conduct/*.md` - Implementation plans, audits, tasks

## 🔍 Finding Code

### Search Patterns

- **Function implementations**: `{function}/typescript/src/` or `{function}/python/{function}/`
- **Tests**: `__tests__/`, `tests/`, `*.test.ts`, `test_*.py`
- **Types**: `types.ts`, `models.py`, `src/types/`
- **Adapters**: `packages/http-*/`, `packages/python-*/`, `adapters/`
- **Examples**: `examples/`, `{function}/examples/`

### Key Directories

```
superfunctions/
├── {function}/              # Core function packages
│   ├── typescript/          # TS implementation
│   ├── python/              # Python implementation
│   ├── .conduct/            # Artifacts
│   ├── README.md            # Documentation
│   └── SPEC.md              # Specification (if exists)
├── packages/                # Shared packages
│   ├── {name}/              # @superfunctions/{name}
│   └── python-{name}/       # Python shared packages
└── _conduct/                # Root artifacts
```

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety
- Provide Python SDKs for backend-focused functions
- Write comprehensive tests

### Documentation

- Update README.md with usage examples
- Create SPEC.md for complex functions
- Document breaking changes
- Keep artifacts in `.conduct/` folders

### Testing

- Use Vitest for TypeScript
- Use pytest for Python
- Maintain high test coverage
- Test adapters separately

### Versioning

- Follow semantic versioning
- Coordinate versions across language SDKs
- Document migration guides for breaking changes

## 🔗 Related Resources

- **Repository**: https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions
- **License**: MIT (most packages) / Apache-2.0 (some packages)
- **Organization**: 21n
- **Contact**: hello@21n.org

## 📝 Notes for AI Agents

1. **Always check both TypeScript and Python** implementations when working on core functions
2. **Respect the naming conventions** - shared packages use `@superfunctions/`, functions use simple names
3. **Create artifacts in `.conduct/` folders**, not in root or arbitrary locations
4. **Avoid nested monorepos** - use subfolders within the main Turbo monorepo
5. **Use Turbo commands** for cross-package operations
6. **Check existing patterns** in similar functions before implementing new features
7. **Maintain consistency** across TypeScript and Python SDKs
8. **Update workspaces** in root `package.json` when adding new packages
9. **Follow existing test patterns** (Vitest for TS, pytest for Python)
10. **Document thoroughly** - this is a developer-focused ecosystem

---

**Last Updated**: 2026-01-12
**Monorepo Version**: 0.1.0
**Package Manager**: npm@10.2.0
**Build Tool**: Turbo v2.0.0

skills.name: Report and Fix PR
skills.summary: Generate a traceable GitHub pull request analysis report from automated review feedback, then fix every reported critical, medium, and low issue in the current worktree and return exact outcome statuses. Use when asked to analyze and remediate PR review feedback end to end, create a `.conduct/pr-reports` report before fixing, or combine PR reporting with PR fixes.

skills.name: Work Linear Issue
skills.summary: Execute an existing Linear issue supplied by a master or orchestrating agent: read the complete issue and discussion, ask blocking clarifications, implement and verify locally, report completion on Linear, then only after explicit master approval create an exact issue-ID branch and open a pull request into the repository default branch.

skills.name: Post Update on Slack
skills.summary: Post a concise update to the correct project Slack channel when the master explicitly requests it. Use when an agent is asked to post, send, or share a project update in Slack; if the master does not specify content, summarize the agent's latest substantive work or changes from the immediately preceding run, with verified status, links, blockers, and next steps.

skills.name: Issue Fix
skills.summary: Troubleshoot and fix software issues with Linear-backed traceability. Use when a user asks an agent to investigate, debug, troubleshoot, repair, or fix a bug or incident, especially when the resulting change may be committed.

skills.name: Add to Backlog
skills.summary: Capture an agent-thread discussion as a detailed Linear backlog item. Use when the user says add this to the backlog, capture this idea, create a Linear ticket, track this for later, or turn the current discussion into planned work requiring a relevant team, a backlog issue, and linked ideation and architecture documents.

skills.name: Create and Associate Linear Issue
skills.summary: Resolve a Linear project and team, safely create or reuse an issue, associate documents, commits, pull requests, deployments, and other artifacts, recover partial writes, and verify the final state. Use as a shared dependency when another skill or agent workflow needs reliable Linear issue creation or association.

## Objective

Run one traceable PR-review remediation cycle in the current repository: collect live GitHub PR feedback, create a complete analysis report and raw evidence export, fix every actionable issue from that exact report, validate the resulting code, and return an honest issue-status summary.

## Guardrails

- Work from the current repository root.
- Inspect the current branch and staged, unstaged, and untracked state before editing. Preserve all pre-existing user changes and avoid overwriting unrelated work.
- Treat GitHub as read-only. Do not post comments, submit reviews, merge, close, or otherwise mutate the PR.
- Do not stage, commit, push, deploy, or open a pull request.
- Do not edit source code until the report and raw export have been written and validated.
- Never invent review tools, issues, severities, files, line numbers, counts, fixes, test results, or completion states.
- Use repository-relative paths in generated artifacts. Exclude local absolute paths, usernames, hostnames, and other machine-specific data.
